opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so "it from qubit" is really an evolution of John Wheeler's old "it from bit" idea, the notion that at the most fundamental level, physical reality, the "it," emerges from information. The quantum version says the fundamental substrate isn't classical bits but quantum information: qubits, entanglement, quantum error correction.

The way I understand it, and the way a lot of us in quantum gravity and quantum information came to see it over the past decade or so, is that spacetime itself might be an emergent phenomenon. It's not the stage on which physics happens. It's something that comes out of the entanglement structure of an underlying quantum system. The cleanest example is AdS/CFT, the holographic correspondence. You have a quantum field theory living on a boundary, and somehow a gravitational theory in a higher-dimensional bulk is encoded in it. Results like Ryu–Takayanagi tell you that the area of certain surfaces in the bulk geometry corresponds to the entanglement entropy of regions on the boundary. So geometry is literally measuring entanglement.

Then you get ideas like Van Raamsdonk's: if you dial down the entanglement between two regions, the spacetime connecting them pinches off. Entanglement is the glue holding spacetime together. And ER=EPR, from Maldacena and Susskind, pushes that further, suggesting wormholes and entangled pairs are two descriptions of the same thing.

What I find really compelling is the connection to quantum error correction. The bulk is encoded in the boundary redundantly, the way a quantum error-correcting code protects logical information across many physical qubits. That explains why you can reconstruct a bulk region from different parts of the boundary. Spacetime starts to look like a code, a kind of tensor network, with geometry reflecting the structure of the circuit.

So my take is that it's a computational view of physics. The universe is fundamentally a quantum computation, and things like geometry, gravity, maybe even locality are emergent, coarse-grained descriptions of how quantum information is organized and processed. That's partly why I moved into quantum machine learning. If physics is quantum information processing, then learning representations of quantum systems, and having quantum computers learn them, becomes a tool for doing fundamental physics. You're using quantum computers to discover the effective theories that emerge from the underlying quantum substrate.

There are still big open questions. Our universe isn't anti-de Sitter, it looks more like de Sitter, and we don't have a clean holographic dictionary there. But as a research program, it from qubit has been one of the most productive reframings of fundamental physics in a long time, because it turns questions about gravity into questions about information, and those are questions we can attack, simulate, and maybe eventually test on actual quantum hardware.

r001.rationale: It presents physical reality as emerging from quantum information—qubits and entanglement—and frames this as a way to recast fundamental physics.

r002.rationale: It calls the universe a quantum computation, but does not describe it as a single quantum computer executing a program or simulating itself.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so "it from qubit" is really the modern descendant of Wheeler's "it from bit." Wheeler's original idea was that physical reality, the "it," at some fundamental level emerges from information, from yes-no answers, from bits. The quantum version says, okay, but the world is quantum mechanical, so the substrate isn't classical bits, it's qubits, and more precisely it's the pattern of entanglement between those qubits.

The way I think about it is that spacetime itself is not fundamental. Geometry is emergent. And what it emerges from is the entanglement structure of some underlying quantum system. The cleanest evidence for this comes out of AdS/CFT and holography. You have the Ryu-Takayanagi formula, where the entanglement entropy of a region on the boundary theory is given by the area of a minimal surface in the bulk. So entanglement entropy on one side literally becomes geometry on the other side. And then you have Van Raamsdonk's work showing that if you dial down the entanglement between two parts of the boundary, the bulk spacetime connecting them literally pinches off and disconnects. Entanglement is what's stitching space together.

Then there's the tensor network picture, which is where my own background comes in. If you take something like MERA, the multi-scale entanglement renormalization ansatz, and you look at the network you're building to represent the ground state of a critical system, the graph structure of that network looks like a discretized slice of anti-de Sitter space. The renormalization direction becomes the radial direction. So you can almost read the holographic dimension as "scale," as coarse-graining depth. And the quantum error-correcting code interpretation, the HaPPY code and that line of work, tells you the bulk degrees of freedom are encoded redundantly in the boundary, which is exactly why you get things like locality and why you can lose part of the boundary and still reconstruct the interior.

So for me the "it from qubit" program is essentially saying: the fundamental theory is a quantum information theory. Gravity, geometry, locality, maybe even time, are all compression artifacts, so to speak. They're the emergent description you get when you look at a highly entangled quantum system at coarse scales. And what I find compelling about it is that it reframes the question of quantum gravity from "how do we quantize the metric" to "what class of quantum circuits or quantum codes produces something that looks like our spacetime," which is a question you can actually attack computationally. It connects quantum computing, condensed matter, and high-energy physics into one language, which is why so many people from very different backgrounds have converged on it.

r001.rationale: It describes the program as saying “the fundamental theory is a quantum information theory” and connects quantum computing, condensed matter, and high-energy physics in one language.

r002.rationale: It discusses quantum systems, circuits, and codes, but does not characterize the universe as one quantum computer executing a program or simulating itself.

astra-6.text:
The way I understand “it from qubits” is that quantum information is the starting point, and spacetime and matter are things you want to recover from it. Usually, we imagine a spacetime and then put quantum systems in it. Here, you ask whether the relationships between quantum degrees of freedom—particularly their entanglement—could give rise to the geometry itself.

A key motivation comes from holography. In certain settings, a theory with gravity can be described by a quantum theory without gravity living on its boundary. Features of the gravitational geometry are related to entanglement in that boundary theory. That suggests geometry and quantum information might be two descriptions of the same underlying structure.

But you need more than a collection of qubits. You need to explain their dynamics, why locality emerges, and why the resulting spacetime obeys something like Einstein’s equations. So I’d describe it as a research program rather than a finished unification: can we derive the gravitational world from the organization and dynamics of quantum information?

r001.rationale: It presents quantum information as the starting point and asks whether spacetime and matter can be recovered from its organization and dynamics, describing this as a unification research program.

r002.rationale: It does not characterize the universe as a single quantum computer executing a program or simulating itself.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about “it from qubits” is that quantum information is more fundamental than the spacetime picture we normally start with. Rather than putting quantum systems into a pre-existing geometry, you ask whether the geometry itself can emerge from the structure of quantum states—their entanglement and the way information is encoded.

Holography gives us a particularly concrete setting for that idea. You can have a quantum theory without gravity that has an equivalent description in terms of a higher-dimensional gravitational spacetime. Entanglement in one description is related to geometric quantities in the other. So something that looks like a distance or an area on the gravity side can have an information-theoretic interpretation on the quantum side.

Quantum error correction is another important part of the story. Information about the gravitational interior seems to be encoded redundantly in the underlying quantum system. That gives us a language for understanding how a spacetime can be robust even though its microscopic constituents are quantum mechanical.

I wouldn’t say that this is already a complete unification of physics. It’s more a change in what we take as fundamental, with some very powerful examples behind it. The question becomes: what kinds of quantum information processing give rise to a world that looks like spacetime, with locality, gravity, and the other physics we observe?

r001.rationale: The response presents quantum information as more fundamental than spacetime and describes geometry emerging from quantum states and information, clearly framing this as the unifying approach.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe the universe as one quantum computer executing a program or simulating itself.
